question: The new policy will significantly reduce carbon emissions.

options.text: The new policy will substantially cut greenhouse gas output.
The new policy will slightly increase carbon emissions.
The new policy will monitor carbon emissions closely.

answer: The new policy will substantially cut greenhouse gas output.
explanation: "Significantly reduce" and "substantially cut" both mean a large decrease. "Carbon emissions" and "greenhouse gas output" refer to the same thing.

question: Researchers discovered a surprising link between diet and memory.

options.text: Scientists uncovered an unexpected connection between what people eat and their recall ability.
Scientists ruled out any connection between diet and memory.
Scientists confirmed an already well-known link between diet and memory.

answer: Scientists uncovered an unexpected connection between what people eat and their recall ability.
explanation: Three separate words are swapped for near-synonyms while the core claim stays identical.

question: The library is currently short-staffed.

options.text: The library doesn't have enough people working there at the moment.
The library has just hired several new staff.
The library is closed for staff training.

answer: The library doesn't have enough people working there at the moment.

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: doesn't have enough people working there

explanation: "Short-staffed" is a single compound word that gets unpacked into a full phrase in speech — a very common IELTS Listening pattern.

question: The committee reached a unanimous decision.

options.text: Every member of the committee agreed on the same outcome.
The committee was unable to agree.
Most, but not all, committee members agreed.

answer: Every member of the committee agreed on the same outcome.

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: every member agreed on the same outcome

explanation: "Unanimous" is a common IELTS vocabulary trap — it means ALL, not most. The paraphrase makes this explicit.

question: Please arrive promptly for your interview.

options.text: Make sure you get there right on time for your interview.
You can arrive any time before your interview.
Your interview has been postponed.

answer: Make sure you get there right on time for your interview.
explanation: "Promptly" is frequently paraphrased as "on time" or "right on time" in Listening recordings.

question: The findings of the study remain inconclusive.

options.text: The study has not produced a clear answer either way.
The study proved its hypothesis beyond doubt.
The study was abandoned before completion.

answer: The study has not produced a clear answer either way.

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: not produced a clear answer either way

explanation: "Inconclusive" is an academic-register word candidates should recognise even when paraphrased into plainer language.

question: The company increased its staff.

options.text: The company expanded its workforce.
The company reduced its workforce.
The company outsourced its workforce.

answer: The company expanded its workforce.
explanation: Verb + noun pair both swapped for close synonyms; direction of change (up) is preserved.

question: The council will postpone the road works.

options.text: The council is going to put off the road works.
The council is going to bring forward the road works.
The council is going to cancel the road works permanently.

answer: The council is going to put off the road works.
explanation: "Postpone" and "put off" both mean delay to a later date, not cancel — a common trap in the distractor options.

question: Sales declined sharply in the final quarter.

options.text: Sales fell dramatically in the last three months of the year.
Sales rose dramatically in the last three months of the year.
Sales remained flat in the last three months of the year.

answer: Sales fell dramatically in the last three months of the year.

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: last three months of the year

explanation: "Quarter" as a business term is unpacked into "three months" — a very common Reading paraphrase for numeric/temporal terms.

question: The tutor will assess your first draft.

options.text: The tutor is going to evaluate your first draft.
The tutor is going to write your first draft.
The tutor is going to ignore your first draft.

answer: The tutor is going to evaluate your first draft.
explanation: Academic verbs like "assess" are often swapped for close synonyms such as "evaluate" or "review".

question: The government plans to phase out single-use plastics by 2027.

options.text: The government intends to gradually eliminate single-use plastics by 2027.
The government intends to immediately ban single-use plastics by 2027.
The government intends to promote single-use plastics until 2027.

answer: The government intends to gradually eliminate single-use plastics by 2027.
explanation: "Phase out" specifically implies a gradual process, which the distractor "immediately ban" contradicts.

question: There was a delay.

options.text: The train was held up.
The train arrived early.
The train was cancelled.

answer: The train was held up.
explanation: The noun "delay" becomes the phrasal verb "held up" — the same event described with a different part of speech.

question: There has been a noticeable improvement in air quality.

options.text: Air quality has clearly got better.
Air quality has clearly got worse.
Air quality has stayed exactly the same.

answer: Air quality has clearly got better.
explanation: The noun phrase "a noticeable improvement in X" becomes the clause "X has clearly got better" — a classic noun-to-verb restructure.

question: There's been a change of venue for tomorrow's talk.

options.text: Tomorrow's talk is being held somewhere different now.
Tomorrow's talk has been cancelled.
Tomorrow's talk is happening earlier than planned.

answer: Tomorrow's talk is being held somewhere different now.
explanation: "Venue" is a high-frequency IELTS noun; recognise it whether it appears as a noun or is paraphrased into a full clause.

question: The rise in youth unemployment is a growing concern.

options.text: People are increasingly worried that more young people can't find work.
People are increasingly relieved that youth unemployment has fallen.
Nobody is particularly concerned about youth unemployment.

answer: People are increasingly worried that more young people can't find work.

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: more young people can't find work

explanation: Two noun phrases are both restructured into full clauses while keeping the negative trend and the concern intact.

question: Students must submit the form before Friday.

options.text: The form has to be handed in by Friday.
The form does not need to be handed in by Friday.
The form was handed in last Friday.

answer: The form has to be handed in by Friday.

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: the form has to be handed in

explanation: Active voice with a human subject becomes passive voice with the form as the subject — same obligation, same deadline.

question: You don't need to book in advance.

options.text: Booking ahead isn't necessary.
You must book ahead.
Bookings are no longer accepted.

answer: Booking ahead isn't necessary.
explanation: The modal structure "don't need to" is rephrased as "isn't necessary" with the verb turned into a gerund subject.

question: Although the budget was tight, the project succeeded.

options.text: Despite a limited budget, the project was successful.
Because the budget was tight, the project failed.
Once the budget increased, the project succeeded.

answer: Despite a limited budget, the project was successful.
explanation: "Although + clause" becomes "despite + noun phrase" — a common concession-structure swap in Reading passages.

question: If you arrive late, you won't be allowed in.

options.text: Late arrivals won't be let in.
Late arrivals will be let in quietly.
Arriving early guarantees entry.

answer: Late arrivals won't be let in.
explanation: A conditional clause is compressed into a noun phrase ("late arrivals") while the consequence stays the same.

question: The report was written by a team of independent researchers.

options.text: A team of independent researchers wrote the report.
A team of independent researchers reviewed the report after it was written.
The report was commissioned by a team of independent researchers.

answer: A team of independent researchers wrote the report.
explanation: Passive-to-active transformation; the doer of the action (the researchers) and the action (writing) stay identical.

question: The hotel is located near the railway station.

options.text: You'll find the hotel just a short walk from the railway station.
You'll find the hotel a long drive from the railway station.
The railway station is inside the hotel.

answer: You'll find the hotel just a short walk from the railway station.
explanation: The whole sentence is rebuilt around "you'll find" instead of "is located" — same fact, different sentence shape.

question: Not everyone enjoyed the lecture.

options.text: Some people found the lecture a bit boring.
Everyone thoroughly enjoyed the lecture.
Nobody attended the lecture.

answer: Some people found the lecture a bit boring.

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: some people found it a bit boring

explanation: A negated universal ("not everyone") is reworded as a positive statement about "some people" — same partial-negative meaning.

question: It is unlikely that the deadline will be extended.

options.text: The deadline will probably stay as it is.
The deadline will almost certainly be extended.
There is no deadline anymore.

answer: The deadline will probably stay as it is.

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: will probably stay as it is

explanation: A negative probability statement is flipped into a positive one with equivalent likelihood — a frequent IELTS trap.

question: Parking is only available to staff, not visitors.

options.text: Only staff can park here — visitors need to look elsewhere.
Both staff and visitors can park here.
Only visitors can park here.

answer: Only staff can park here — visitors need to look elsewhere.
explanation: The exclusion ("not visitors") is restructured as an instruction ("need to look elsewhere") while keeping the same restriction.

question: The museum opens at 9:30.
context: We originally planned to open at nine, but we've changed the schedule. The museum will begin admitting visitors at half past nine.

options.text: half past nine
nine o'clock
quarter past nine

answer: half past nine
explanation: "Nine o'clock" is mentioned first but is then corrected — the final, changed information is what's tested, not the first number you hear.

question: How much does the standard membership cost?
context: The premium membership is £120 a year, though most people actually go for the standard one, which is just £75.
explanation: £120 refers to a different membership tier (premium) mentioned first — a classic "correct number, wrong category" distractor.

question: Where should new students go first on orientation day?
context: New students used to report to the main hall, but that's changed this year — head to the library entrance instead.

options.text: the library entrance
the main hall
the student office

answer: the library entrance
explanation: "Used to" signals outdated information; the current, correct instruction always comes after this kind of correction language.

question: What time does the workshop actually start?
context: It says 2pm on the flyer, but that's wrong — we pushed it back to 3pm because of the room booking.

options.text: 3pm
2pm
4pm

answer: 3pm
explanation: Printed/written information is explicitly corrected by the speaker — always trust the spoken correction over the first number given.

question: According to the passage, what caused the delay in construction?
context: Some early reports blamed bad weather for the delay, but the final inquiry found the real cause was a shortage of materials.

options.text: a shortage of materials
bad weather
a lack of workers

answer: a shortage of materials

key_paraphrases.paraphrase: the real cause was a shortage of materials

explanation: Reading passages often present an initial claim before overturning it — the final, confirmed statement is what answers the question.

question: Which room is the seminar being held in?
context: Room 4 is being used for something else today, so we've moved the seminar to Room 7 instead.

options.text: Room 7
Room 4
Room 9

answer: Room 7
explanation: Room 4 is mentioned only to explain why the venue changed — it is never the answer itself.
